Annual use is generally capped at net income tax minus the greater of tentative minimum tax or 25% of tax above $25,000; unused credits carry back 1 year and forward 20 years.
Executive Summary and Statutory Architecture

The General Business Credit (GBC), codified under Title 26 of the United States Code, Section 38 (IRC § 38), serves as the central statutory aggregation and limitation framework governing the utilization of federal business tax incentives. Rather than operating as an independent, substantive tax credit generated by a single business activity, the GBC functions as an umbrella pooling mechanism. Under IRC § 38(a), a taxpayer's allowable GBC for any taxable year is defined as the sum of three distinct pools: the business credit carryforwards carried to that taxable year under IRC § 38(a)(1), the amount of the current year business credit determined under IRC § 38(a)(2), plus the business credit carrybacks carried to that taxable year under IRC § 38(a)(3). By consolidating disparate incentives enumerated under IRC § 38(b) into a unified credit basket, the statutory architecture enforces a single annual tax liability ceiling under IRC § 38(c).

Within this statutory framework, the Credit for Increasing Research Activities—commonly referred to as the Research and Development (R&D) Tax Credit under IRC § 41—represents one of the primary domestic incentives channeled through the GBC mechanism. While IRC § 41 establishes the substantive qualification criteria and incremental calculation formulas for research expenditures, IRC § 38 dictates the extent to which that calculated credit can be monetized against federal income tax liability in a given year. Because the GBC is fundamentally non-refundable under standard income tax rules, any credit amount exceeding the statutory ceiling imposed by IRC § 38(c) cannot be refunded directly as cash (absent specific statutory elections for certain clean energy credits under IRC § 6417 or small business payroll tax credits under IRC §§ 41(h) and 3111(f)) and instead converts into an unused business credit governed by the carryover regime of IRC § 39.
Statutory Foundation and Multi-Form Compliance Mechanics
Enumeration of Component Credits Under IRC § 38(b)

The legislative rationale for aggregating business tax credits under IRC § 38(b) is to prevent taxpayers from stacking multiple standalone non-refundable credits to eliminate their entire federal income tax liability simultaneously. Under Subpart D of Part IV, Subchapter A, Chapter 1 of Subtitle A of the Internal Revenue Code, IRC § 38(b)(1)–(41) enumerates 41 distinct component credits that constitute the current year business credit. These component incentives span capital investment, employment, research, low-income housing, agricultural and industrial production, and clean energy generation.

Technical Reporting Architecture and Form 3800 Sequencing

Compliance with IRC § 38 requires a structured two-tier reporting process. Taxpayers first compute each substantive incentive on its dedicated source form—such as Form 6765 for the IRC § 41 research credit or Form 3468 for the IRC § 46 investment credit—and subsequently transfer the resulting credit amounts to Form 3800 (General Business Credit). Following the comprehensive redesign of Form 3800 beginning in tax year 2023 and continuing through the 2025 revision to accommodate the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 (IRA 2022) and the CHIPS Act of 2022, taxpayers must complete Parts III, IV, V, and VI (as applicable) before computing the final tax liability limitation in Parts I and II. Specifically, Part III reports all current-year general business credits (separating passive activity credits in columns (d)(1)–(d)(4), non-passive credits in columns (e)–(f)(2), IRC § 6417 or § 48D gross and net elective payment elections in columns (h) and (j), and tax offsets in column (i)), while Part IV tracks all carryforwards and carrybacks of unused credits. Parts V and VI provide facility-by-facility and pass-through entity breakdowns when a filer has multiple IRS registration numbers or multiple Schedules K-1 for a single credit. Furthermore, taxpayers executing credit transfers under IRC § 6418 must attach Schedule A (Form 3800), Transfer Election Statement (or a compliant standalone purchase and sale agreement saved as a PDF named "Transfer Election Statement"), obtain pre-filing IRS registration numbers for each eligible facility or property prior to filing, and ensure both transferor and transferee sign the attestation under Lines 13a and 13b.

General business credits reported on Form 3800 are consumed on a first-in, first-out (FIFO) basis across tax years. Specifically, for any given taxable year, the tax liability limitation is absorbed first by business credit carryforwards to that taxable year (reported on Part II, Line 34) applied in chronological order starting with the earliest unused credit year first, second by the current year business credit earned in that taxable year (reported on Part III or Part V), and third by business credit carrybacks carried to that taxable year from a subsequent unused credit year (reported on Part II, Line 35).

When aggregate credits within a single taxable year exceed the allowable tax liability limitation, IRC § 38(d)(1)–(2) and the IRS Instructions for Form 3800 enforce a mandatory intra-year statutory credit ordering rule determined by the order in which the credits are listed in IRC § 38(b) as of the close of the taxable year in which the credit is used. Under IRC § 38(d)(2) and Form 3800 instructions, utilization begins first with the IRC § 46 investment credit (ordered internally by the rehabilitation credit, energy credit, qualifying advanced coal project credit, qualifying gasification project credit, qualifying advanced energy project credit, qualifying therapeutic discovery project credit carryforward, and advanced manufacturing investment credit), followed sequentially by the work opportunity credit (Form 5884), the alcohol fuels/biofuel producer credit (Form 6478), the credit for increasing research activities (Form 6765), the low-income housing credit (Form 8586), the enhanced oil recovery credit (Form 8830), the disabled access credit (Form 8826), the renewable electricity production credit (Form 8835), the empowerment zone employment credit (Form 8844), and subsequent IRC § 38(b) credits. Additionally, Form 3800 segregates credits into distinct utilization buckets based on whether the credit is disallowed against the Tentative Minimum Tax (TMT) floor (reported in Part I) or qualifies under Part II (Sections A, B, and C) as a credit subject to the general IRC § 38(c)(1) limitation, an empowerment zone employment credit under IRC § 38(c)(2), or a "specified credit" under IRC § 38(c)(4) that may offset TMT.
GBC Limitation Mechanics and the Non-Refundability Ceiling
The Statutory Limitation Formula Under IRC § 38(c)(1)

The core statutory constraint governing GBC monetization is codified in IRC § 38(c)(1). Under the general rule of IRC § 38(c)(1), the general business credit allowed under IRC § 38(a) for any taxable year shall not exceed the excess (if any) of the taxpayer's net income tax over the greater of two limiting factors: under subparagraph (A), the tentative minimum tax for the taxable year, or under subparagraph (B), 25 percent of so much of the taxpayer's net regular tax liability as exceeds $25,000.

In this statutory equation, IRC § 38(c)(1) defines both tax base variables with precision. Net Income Tax (NIT) is defined as the sum of the taxpayer's regular tax liability and the alternative minimum tax (AMT) imposed by IRC § 55, reduced by the non-refundable personal and foreign or other credits allowable under Subparts A and B of Part IV (such as the foreign tax credit under IRC § 27). Net Regular Tax Liability (NRTL) is correspondingly defined as the taxpayer's regular tax liability reduced by the sum of the credits allowable under Subparts A and B of Part IV.
Corporate Application Under IRC § 38(c)(6)(E) and TMT Exceptions

First, while the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017 repealed the historical corporate AMT, the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 enacted the Corporate Alternative Minimum Tax (CAMT) under IRC § 55 for applicable large corporations, and Item A of Form 3800 along with its instructions explicitly require corporate taxpayers to report CAMT status and define corporate "net income tax" as "the sum of the regular tax liability and the tax imposed by the alternative minimum tax under section 55, reduced by certain other credits". Second, the statutory reason C corporations do not apply the two-prong "greater of TMT or 25% of net regular tax liability over $25,000" test is codified directly in IRC § 38(c)(6)(E) ("Corporations"). Under IRC § 38(c)(6)(E)(i)–(iii), for any corporation, the first sentence of IRC § 38(c)(1) is applied by substituting "25 percent of the taxpayer's net income tax as exceeds $25,000" in place of "the greater of" and all that follows, and paragraphs (2)(A) and (4)(A) of IRC § 38(c) are applied without regard to clause (ii)(I) thereof. Consequently, for a C corporation, the statutory limitation formula simplifies to 75 percent of net income tax above $25,000 (plus 100 percent of the first $25,000):

Furthermore, for non-corporate taxpayers (such as individuals, estates, trusts, and pass-through owners) who remain subject to the two-prong test of IRC § 38(c)(1), the statute provides two targeted modifications to the TMT barrier. Under the first modification in IRC § 38(c)(4)(A) governing specified credits, IRC §§ 38 and 39 are applied separately with respect to such credits, the tentative minimum tax is statutorily treated as being zero under clause (ii)(I), and the IRC § 38(c)(1) limitation (as modified) is reduced by the non-specified credits allowed under IRC § 38(a) for the taxable year under clause (ii)(II). Under IRC § 38(c)(4)(B)(i)–(xii), specified credits include: (i) the alcohol fuels credit under IRC § 40 for tax years beginning after December 31, 2004; (ii) the research credit determined under IRC § 41 for an eligible small business; (iii) the low-income housing credit under IRC § 42 attributable to buildings placed in service after December 31, 2007; (iv) the renewable electricity or refined coal production credit under IRC § 45 during the 4-year period beginning on the date the facility was originally placed in service; (v) the Indian coal production credit under IRC § 45(e)(10); (vi) the employer Social Security tip credit under IRC § 45B; (vii) the railroad track maintenance credit under IRC § 45G; (viii) the small employer health insurance credit under IRC § 45R; (ix) the paid family and medical leave credit under IRC § 45S; (x) the IRC § 46 investment credit attributable to the energy credit under IRC § 48; (xi) the IRC § 46 investment credit attributable to the rehabilitation credit under IRC § 47 for qualified rehabilitation expenditures properly taken into account for periods after December 31, 2007; and (xii) the work opportunity credit under IRC § 51.

Crucially for R&D claimants, under IRC § 38(c)(5)(A) and the IRS Instructions for Form 3800, an "eligible small business" for purposes of treating the IRC § 41 research credit as a specified credit under IRC § 38(c)(4)(B)(ii) is defined as a corporation whose stock is not publicly traded, a partnership, or a sole proprietorship whose average annual gross receipts for the 3-taxable-year period preceding the taxable year do not exceed $50,000,000 (applying rules similar to IRC § 448(c)(2) and (3), including controlled group aggregation under IRC § 52(a)–(b), predecessor inclusion, reduction for returns and allowances, and short-period annualization). Moreover, under IRC § 38(c)(5)(B), a research credit determined with respect to a partnership or S corporation is not treated as a specified credit by any partner or shareholder unless both the pass-through entity and the individual partner or shareholder separately satisfy the $50,000,000 gross receipts test for the taxable year in which the credit is treated as a current year business credit. Under the second modification in IRC § 38(c)(2) governing the empowerment zone employment credit determined under IRC § 1396, the statute substitutes 75 percent of the tentative minimum tax for the full TMT under IRC § 38(c)(1)(A) (reduced by non-specified and non-empowerment-zone credits allowed under IRC § 38(a)), thereby allowing the empowerment zone employment credit to offset up to 25 percent of TMT.
The 75 Percent Marginal Offset Rule and Special $25,000 Apportionment Rules

Because the 25 percent unoffset tax floor applies only to tax liability exceeding $25,000, a taxpayer with a net regular tax liability (or corporate net income tax) of $25,000 or less (and zero TMT) experiences a zero limiting factor and can offset 100 percent of its tax liability with the GBC. Above the $25,000 threshold, the required floor rises by $0.25 for every $1.00 of tax liability, meaning the GBC can offset 75 percent of marginal tax liability exceeding $25,000.

However, IRC § 38(c)(6)(A)–(D) imposes strict anti-abuse and apportionment constraints on the $25,000 floor across specific taxpayer classifications. Under IRC § 38(c)(6)(A), a husband or wife filing a separate return must substitute $12,500 in lieu of $25,000, unless the taxpayer's spouse has no current-year business credit, carryforward, or carryback for, or to, the spouse's taxable year ending within or with the taxpayer's taxable year. Under IRC § 38(c)(6)(B), for a controlled group of corporations (as defined in IRC § 1563(a)), the single $25,000 amount is reduced for each component member by apportioning the $25,000 among the component members in accordance with Treasury regulations. Similarly, under IRC § 38(c)(6)(C), for regulated investment companies and real estate investment trusts described in IRC § 46(e)(1)(A) or (B) (as in effect on the day before the date of enactment of the Revenue Reconciliation Act of 1990), the $25,000 amount equals that person's ratable share (as determined under former IRC § 46(e)(2)). Finally, under IRC § 38(c)(6)(D), for an estate or trust, the $25,000 threshold is reduced to an amount bearing the same ratio to $25,000 as the portion of the estate's or trust's income not allocated to beneficiaries bears to its total income.

Integration of the R&D Tax Credit (IRC § 41) Within the GBC Framework
Incremental Calculation Mechanics Under IRC § 41(a) and § 41(c)

Before an R&D credit enters the Form 3800 aggregation pool, its gross dollar value must be determined under IRC § 41 on Form 6765. To qualify under IRC § 41(d)(1), research activities must satisfy a four-part statutory test: first, the expenditures must qualify as domestic research or experimental expenditures under IRC § 174A; second, the research must be undertaken for the purpose of discovering information that is technological in nature (resting on principles of physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science); third, the application of that information must be intended to be useful in the development of a new or improved business component (product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention) of the taxpayer evaluated by function, performance, reliability, or quality; and fourth, substantially all of the activities must constitute elements of a process of experimentation to resolve technical uncertainty regarding capability, method, or appropriate design. Under the regular credit method of IRC § 41(a), the research credit for a taxable year equals the sum of three components: 20 percent of the excess (if any) of the taxpayer's Qualified Research Expenses (QREs) for the taxable year over the base amount under IRC § 41(a)(1), plus 20 percent of the basic research payments determined under IRC § 41(e)(1)(A) as provided in IRC § 41(a)(2), plus 20 percent of the amounts paid or incurred by the taxpayer in carrying on any trade or business during the taxable year (including contributions) to an energy research consortium for energy research under IRC § 41(a)(3).

Under IRC § 41(c)(3)(A), the historical fixed-base percentage is the ratio of aggregate QREs to aggregate gross receipts for taxable years beginning after December 31, 1983, and before January 1, 1989. Under IRC § 41(c)(3)(B), start-up companies (taxpayers whose first taxable year with both gross receipts and QREs began after December 31, 1983, or that had fewer than 3 taxable years between 1984 and 1988 with both gross receipts and QREs) are assigned a fixed-base percentage of 3 percent for each of the first 5 taxable years beginning after December 31, 1993 for which the taxpayer has QREs, followed by a phased transition from the 6th through 10th such taxable years (one-sixth of the 4th–5th year ratio in year 6; one-third of the 5th–6th year ratio in year 7; one-half of the 5th–7th year ratio in year 8; two-thirds of the 5th–8th year ratio in year 9; five-sixths of the 5th–9th year ratio in year 10; and the ratio from any 5 years selected by the taxpayer among the 5th through 10th years thereafter). Under IRC § 41(c)(3)(C) and (D), the fixed-base percentage is rounded to the nearest 1/100th of 1 percent and is statutorily capped at a maximum fixed-base percentage of 16 percent. Furthermore, IRC § 41(c)(2) enforces a statutory minimum base amount rule providing that in no event shall the base amount be less than 50 percent of the qualified research expenses for the credit year.

Alternatively, under IRC § 41(c)(4)(A), a taxpayer may elect the Alternative Simplified Credit (ASC) on Form 6765, which equals 14 percent of so much of the taxpayer's QREs for the taxable year as exceeds 50 percent of the average QREs for the 3 taxable years preceding the credit year (or, under the special rule of IRC § 41(c)(4)(B), 6 percent of current-year QREs if the taxpayer has no QREs in any one of the 3 preceding taxable years). Additionally, under IRC § 280C(c)(1), a taxpayer claiming the full IRC § 41(a) credit must reduce its domestic research or experimental expenditure deduction (or capital account charge) under IRC § 174A(b) by the amount of the credit allowed, unless the taxpayer makes an irrevocable election on a timely filed original return (Item A of Form 6765) under IRC § 280C(c)(2) (formerly codified at IRC § 280C(c)(3) prior to redesignation by Public Law 119–21) to claim a reduced research credit lessened by the maximum corporate tax rate under IRC § 11(b) (21 percent, yielding 79 percent of the gross credit).
Controlled Group Aggregation Under IRC § 41(f)(1) Versus IRC § 38(c)(6)(B)

For corporate enterprises operating through parent-subsidiary or brother-sister structures, IRC § 41(f)(1) mandates that all members of the same controlled group of corporations and all trades or businesses (whether or not incorporated) under common control shall be treated as a single taxpayer in determining the amount of the research credit. Consequently, all group members must aggregate their QREs, basic research payments, energy research consortium contributions, and historical gross receipts to compute a single group-wide research credit, which is then allocated among the members on a proportionate basis according to each member's share of the aggregate QREs, basic research payments, and energy research consortium amounts taken into account under IRC § 41. Under IRC § 280C(c)(3), the same controlled group aggregation rules govern the application of IRC § 280C(c) across group members.

However, tax planners must also account for the parallel controlled group restriction embedded in IRC § 38(c)(6)(B): members of a controlled group (as defined in IRC § 1563(a)) cannot each claim a separate $25,000 full-offset threshold under IRC § 38(c)(1)(B), but must instead apportion a single $25,000 amount across the entire group in accordance with Treasury regulations.

body.text: Under the amended text of IRC § 174 (as modified by Public Law 119–21, § 70302(b) for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024), mandatory capitalization under IRC § 174 is now restricted specifically to foreign research or experimental expenditures (defined in IRC § 174(b) by reference to foreign research under IRC § 41(d)(4)(F)), which continue to be amortized ratably over a 15-year period beginning with the midpoint of the taxable year. Furthermore, under amended IRC § 174(d), for any property with respect to which foreign R&E expenditures are paid or incurred that is disposed of, retired, or abandoned after May 12, 2025, no deduction or reduction to amount realized is permitted on account of such disposition, retirement, or abandonment, and the 15-year amortization schedule must continue.

Meanwhile, domestic R&E expenditures (including software development under IRC § 174A(d)(3), but excluding land or depreciable/depletable property under § 174A(d)(1) and mineral/oil/gas exploration under § 174A(d)(2)) are permanently governed by newly enacted IRC § 174A. Under IRC § 174A(a), taxpayers may immediately deduct domestic R&E expenditures in the taxable year paid or incurred, or elect under IRC § 174A(c) to capitalize and amortize them over at least 60 months (or over 10 years under IRC § 59(e)). In addition, Section 70302(f) of Public Law 119–21 and IRS Revenue Procedure 2025-28 established two major transition mechanisms for domestic R&E costs capitalized during the 2022–2024 window. Under the first transition rule in Section 70302(f)(1) of Public Law 119–21 governing retroactive small business application, an "eligible taxpayer" (any taxpayer other than a tax shelter under IRC § 448(a)(3) that meets the IRC § 448(c) gross receipts test—average annual gross receipts of $31,000,000 or less for the three prior taxable years—for its first taxable year beginning after December 31, 2024) was permitted to elect by July 6, 2026 (one year after enactment) to apply IRC § 174A retroactively to taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021, via amended returns or a Section 481 change in accounting method, accompanied by a special window under Section 70302(f)(1)(D) to make or revoke an IRC § 280C(c)(2) reduced-credit election for those retroactive years. Under the second transition rule in Section 70302(f)(2) of Public Law 119–21 governing accelerated recovery of pre-2025 unamortized balances, any taxpayer with remaining unamortized domestic R&E expenditures paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021, and before January 1, 2025, may elect to deduct the remaining unamortized balance either in full in the first taxable year beginning after December 31, 2024 (the 2025 return) or ratably over the 2-taxable-year period beginning with the first taxable year beginning after December 31, 2024 (2025 and 2026), treated as a taxpayer-initiated change in method of accounting with automatic IRS consent applied on a cut-off basis with no IRC § 481(a) adjustment.

During the 2022–2024 window (and for taxpayers retaining foreign R&E amortization under IRC § 174), disallowed immediate deductions artificially increased taxable income, Regular Tax Liability, and Net Income Tax (NIT), which expanded the IRC § 38(c) utilization ceiling and absorbed more IRC § 41 credits currently. Conversely, for tax years beginning after December 31, 2024, as taxpayers immediately deduct domestic R&E expenditures under IRC § 174A(a)—and particularly as they deduct 100 percent or 50 percent catch-up installments of unamortized 2022–2024 domestic balances in 2025 and 2026—current-year taxable income and NIT decrease substantially, which simultaneously contracts the IRC § 38(c) utilization ceiling and increases the volume of IRC § 41 credits pushed into IRC § 39 carryforwards.
Management of Excess Credits and Strategic Carve-Outs
Carryback and Carryforward Mechanics Under IRC § 39

When the sum of business credit carryforwards to a taxable year plus the current-year business credit exceeds the IRC § 38(c) limitation for that year (designated statutorily as the "unused credit year"), the excess attributable to the current-year credit becomes an unused business credit governed by IRC § 39. Under the general rule of IRC § 39(a)(1), an unused business credit is carried back 1 taxable year preceding the unused credit year under subparagraph (A), and carried forward to each of the 20 taxable years following the unused credit year under subparagraph (B).

Under IRC § 39(a)(2)(A)–(B), the entire amount of the unused credit must first be carried to the earliest of the 21 taxable years (the 1 preceding carryback year plus the 20 succeeding carryforward years) to which it may be carried, and is then carried sequentially to each of the remaining 20 taxable years to the extent it could not be taken into account under IRC § 38(a) for a prior taxable year due to the limitations of IRC § 39(b) and IRC § 39(c). Under IRC § 39(b), the amount of an unused credit carried back to a preceding year under IRC § 38(a)(3) cannot exceed the excess of that preceding year's IRC § 38(c) limitation over the sum of (1) the carryforwards and current-year credits already determined under IRC § 38(a)(1) and (2) for that preceding year, plus (2) any carrybacks to that preceding year attributable to unused credit years prior to the current unused credit year. Similarly, under IRC § 39(c), the amount of an unused credit carried forward to a succeeding year under IRC § 38(a)(1) cannot exceed the excess of that succeeding year's IRC § 38(c) limitation over the sum of carryforwards to that succeeding year attributable to taxable years preceding the unused credit year. In addition, IRC § 39(d) imposes a transitional restriction prohibiting any portion of an unused business credit attributable to a credit specified in IRC § 38(b) from being carried back to any taxable year before the first taxable year for which that specified credit (or portion thereof) is allowable.

First, under IRC § 39(a)(3), the marginal oil and gas well production credit is applied separately from the general business credit with a 5-year carryback and a 20-year (24-year remaining after the earliest year) carryforward, spanning 25 taxable years in total. Second, under IRC § 39(a)(4), enacted by the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 (Pub. L. 117–169, effective for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2022), clean energy "applicable credits" defined in IRC § 6417(b) are applied separately with a 3-year carryback and a 20-year (22-year remaining after the earliest year) carryforward, spanning 23 taxable years in total.
Deduction for Unused Business Credits Under IRC § 196
To prevent permanent economic forfeiture if an unused credit expires unabsorbed at the end of its 20-year carryforward window, IRC § 196 provides a statutory backstop.

First, rather than operating as a discretionary election, IRC § 196(a) mandates a statutory deduction, providing that if any portion of qualified business credits determined for any taxable year has not, after the application of IRC § 38(c), been allowed to the taxpayer as a credit under IRC § 38 for any taxable year, "an amount equal to the credit not so allowed shall be allowed to the taxpayer as a deduction for the first taxable year following the last taxable year for which such credit could, under section 39, have been allowed as a credit". Furthermore, under IRC § 196(b), if a taxpayer dies or ceases to exist before that first taxable year following the expiration of the IRC § 39 carryforward period, the unallowed amount (or proper portion thereof) is accelerated and allowed as a deduction for the taxable year in which such death or cessation occurs, in accordance with Treasury regulations.

Second, the IRC § 196 deduction is not available to all 41 IRC § 38(b) credits; it applies strictly to the 14 "qualified business credits" enumerated in IRC § 196(c)(1)–(14): (1) the IRC § 46 investment credit (but only to the extent attributable to property the basis of which is reduced by IRC § 50(c)); (2) the IRC § 51(a) work opportunity credit; (3) the IRC § 40(a) alcohol fuels credit; (4) the IRC § 41(a) research credit (other than a reduced credit under IRC § 280C(c)) for taxable years beginning after December 31, 1988; (5) the IRC § 43(a) enhanced oil recovery credit; (6) the IRC § 1396(a) empowerment zone employment credit; (7) the IRC § 45A(a) Indian employment credit; (8) the IRC § 45B(a) employer Social Security credit; (9) the IRC § 45D(a) new markets tax credit; (10) the IRC § 45E(a) small employer pension plan startup cost credit; (11) the IRC § 40A(a) biodiesel fuels credit; (12) the IRC § 45H(a) low sulfur diesel fuel production credit; (13) the IRC § 45L(a) new energy efficient home credit; and (14) the IRC § 45R(a) small employer health insurance credit.

Third, and most importantly for R&D credit claimants, IRC § 196(c)(4) explicitly restricts the expiration deduction to the research credit determined under IRC § 41(a) "other than such credit determined under section 280C(c)(3)" (redesignated as IRC § 280C(c)(2) under Public Law 119–21) for taxable years beginning after December 31, 1988. Because a taxpayer that elects the reduced research credit under IRC § 280C(c)(2) (historically § 280C(c)(3)) already avoided reducing its current-year R&E deduction under IRC § 280C(c)(1) in the year the credit originated, allowing an IRC § 196 deduction upon expiration would confer an impermissible double tax deduction for the same expenditures. Similarly, under IRC § 196(d), for an investment credit determined under IRC § 46 (other than the rehabilitation credit), the expiration deduction under IRC § 196(a) is limited to 50 percent of the unused credit.
The Qualified Small Business (QSB) Payroll Tax Offset Under IRC §§ 41(h) and 3111(f)

To provide immediate cash flow liquidity to startups, the Protecting Americans from Tax Hikes (PATH) Act of 2015 enacted IRC §§ 41(h) and 3111(f), establishing the Qualified Small Business (QSB) Payroll Tax Credit for Increasing Research Activities, which was subsequently expanded by Provision 13902 of the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022.

body.text: Under IRC § 41(h)(2), for any taxable year, the "payroll tax credit portion" of the research credit determined under IRC § 41(a) is the least of: (A) the amount specified in the taxpayer's payroll tax election, (B) the research credit determined under IRC § 41(a) for the taxable year (before the application of IRC § 41(h)), or (C) in the case of a qualified small business other than a partnership or S corporation, the amount of the business credit carryforward under IRC § 39 carried from that taxable year (determined before the application of IRC § 41(h)). Under IRC § 41(h)(4)(A) and IRS administrative guidance (Notice 2017-23 and the Instructions for Form 6765, Form 3800, and Form 8974), the election must be made on Form 6765 (Line 36, or Line 44 for tax years beginning before January 1, 2024) attached to a timely filed original return (including extensions)—at the entity level for a partnership (Form 1065 under IRC § 6031) or S corporation (Form 1120-S under IRC § 6037) under IRC § 41(h)(4)(C)—cannot be made on an amended return, and may be revoked only with the consent of the Secretary. Under IRC § 41(h)(1) and the IRS Instructions for Form 3800, the elected payroll tax credit portion is not treated as an income tax credit under IRC § 41(a) (other than for purposes of the IRC § 280C deduction reduction), cannot offset current-year income tax liability, and must be subtracted from any research credit carryforward reported on Form 3800, Part II, Line 34.

Once elected, the credit is claimed on Form 8974 attached to Form 941 (Employer's Quarterly Federal Tax Return, or annual Forms 943/944) starting in the first calendar quarter that begins after the date the QSB files its income tax return reflecting the election. On Form 8974, Part 2, Line 12 applies the credit against the employer's 50 percent share of Social Security tax up to $250,000 per quarter, Line 16 applies any remaining credit (Line 13) against the employer's 50 percent share of Medicare tax (Line 15), and Line 17 transfers the combined credit to Form 941, Line 11. Businesses utilizing a Section 3504 agent, a Certified Professional Employer Organization (CPEO), or a non-certified PEO claim the credit on the aggregate Form 941 filed under the agent's, CPEO's, or PEO's EIN, supported by Schedule R (Form 941) (Allocation Schedule for Aggregate Form 941 Filers) and a separate Form 8974 for each electing QSB client.

Specifically, under IRC § 41(h)(3)(A)(i)–(ii), a corporation, partnership, or other person (excluding tax-exempt organizations under IRC § 501 per § 41(h)(3)(B)) qualifies as a "qualified small business" for the payroll tax offset only if: (I) its gross receipts (as determined under the computation rules of IRC § 448(c)(3), without regard to subparagraph (A) thereof) for the taxable year are less than $5,000,000, and (II) it did not have gross receipts (as so determined) for any taxable year preceding the 5-taxable-year period ending with such taxable year. In addition, under IRC § 41(h)(4)(B)(ii), a taxpayer may not make the payroll tax election if the taxpayer (or any person aggregated as a single taxpayer under IRC § 41(h)(5)(A) and § 41(f)(1)) has made an election under IRC § 41(h) for 5 or more preceding taxable years. Under IRC § 41(h)(5)(A)–(B), all members of a controlled group or businesses under common control are aggregated as a single taxpayer for the $5,000,000 gross receipts test and the 5-year test, and the $500,000 annual election cap (each of the two $250,000 amounts in § 41(h)(4)(B)(i)) is allocated proportionately among the members in the same manner as under IRC § 41(f)(1). Because IRC § 41(h)(3)(A)(i)(I) cross-references only the computational mechanics of IRC § 448(c)(3) (such as short-year annualization and reduction for returns and allowances) while imposing its own hard statutory ceiling of less than $5,000,000 for the current taxable year, startups with current-year gross receipts of $5,000,000 or more are statutorily ineligible for the IRC § 41(h) payroll tax offset.
Strategic Conclusions and Analytical Recommendations

Because IRC § 38(c) caps annual utilization at Net Income Tax less the 25 percent floor above $25,000 (or TMT for non-specified credits of non-corporate taxpayers), high-R&D enterprises routinely accumulate substantial credit carryforwards that require multi-decade tax planning.

First, tax departments should construct multi-scenario sensitivity models of the IRC § 38(c) ceiling across IRC §§ 174 and 174A regimes to quantify how shifts in the taxable income base alter credit absorption. Specifically, following the enactment of Public Law 119–21 (signed July 4, 2025) and IRC § 174A, taxpayers transitioning out of mandatory 5-year domestic R&E amortization for tax years beginning after December 31, 2024—or electing under Section 70302(f)(2) of Public Law 119–21 and Rev. Proc. 2025-28 to deduct unamortized 2022–2024 domestic R&E balances in full in 2025 or ratably across 2025 and 2026—must model the resulting compression of their Net Income Tax (NIT) and the corresponding reduction in current-year GBC absorption capacity. Where immediate domestic expensing under IRC § 174A(a) would eliminate current-year tax liability and trap expiring GBC carryforwards, planners should evaluate whether electing 60-month amortization under IRC § 174A(c) or 10-year amortization under IRC § 59(e) preserves sufficient NIT to absorb older credit vintages.

Crucially, this tracker must record whether the taxpayer elected the 21 percent reduced research credit under IRC § 280C(c)(2) (formerly IRC § 280C(c)(3)) in each origination year, as only unreduced IRC § 41(a) credits qualify for the mandatory Year 21 expiration deduction (or earlier cessation deduction) under IRC § 196(a)–(c)(4).

Third, tax advisors should implement integrated 5-year startup liquidity and 20-year corporate utilization forecasting. For early-stage enterprises that satisfy the strict IRC § 41(h)(3)(A) QSB eligibility criteria (under $5,000,000 in current-year gross receipts and no gross receipts prior to the 5-taxable-year period ending with the credit year), tax planners must align Form 6765 elections on timely filed original returns with quarterly Form 8974 and Form 941 payroll tax liabilities to capture up to $500,000 annually ($250,000 per quarter against employer Social Security tax on Form 8974, Line 12, plus remaining excess against employer Medicare tax on Line 16). For established corporations and controlled groups subject to the single apportioned $25,000 threshold under IRC § 38(c)(6)(B), 5-year and 20-year capital budgeting forecasts must pair projected QRE growth under IRC § 41(f)(1) with projected Net Income Tax and Corporate Alternative Minimum Tax (CAMT) trajectories to prevent credit expiration at the end of the IRC § 39 carryforward horizon.
